name: fierce
purpose: Lightweight DNS scanner that finds hostnames and non-contiguous IP space: NS/SOA lookup, zone transfer attempt, wildcard check, subdomain brute force, then reverse (PTR) lookups on the IPs next to every hit
author: Robert 'RSnake' Hansen (original Perl, with id, Vacuum, Robert E Lee and IceShaman); mschwager (Python 3 port)
why_notable: Robert 'RSnake' Hansen of ha.ckers.org wrote fierce.pl (copyright 2006, released 20 February 2007) out of frustration after a web application audit: a company's hosts are spread across unrelated netblocks, so scanning 'their /24' misses most of them. Fierce's answer was to pivot through reverse DNS: after checking the NS and SOA, trying a zone transfer and testing for wildcard DNS (which would make every guess resolve), it brute-forces subdomains and, for every hit, looks up the PTR records of the neighbouring IPs, revealing hosts such as jenkins or vpn-old that no wordlist contains. The phrase 'non-contiguous IP space' became the stated goal of dnsenum too, and SecLists still ships fierce-hostlist.txt. Matt Schwager (mschwager) later ported it to Python 3 under GPL-3.0 to simplify and modernise the codebase; that port, maintained until about 2024 and continued in forks, is what pip, Kali and Debian ship (Debian also keeps the original fierce.pl). Its flags changed with the port (--domain instead of -dns), it runs lookups sequentially (multiprocessing is still a README TODO), and it has no JSON output, so it suits depth rather than million-word lists. Pentesters run it after the main enumeration and internally (--dns-servers <DC> --range) to map networks through PTRs without port scanning; bug bounty hunters use the neighbour walk to find forgotten infrastructure; DNS engineers learn how much descriptive PTR names leak; SOC analysts recognise its small clusters of sequential in-addr.arpa queries; and it appears in CEH, OSCP and CPTS DNS sections.
